title: Rule of 0 / 3 / 5
html:
If a class needs a custom destructor, copy or move operation, it almost certainly needs all of them. Better still: design so it needs none.

The rules

Rule of Three (C++98)

If you define any of destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, define all three.

Rule of Five (C++11)

Add move constructor and move assignment: define or =delete all five together.

Rule of Zero

Don't manage resources by hand. Use members that manage themselves (std::string, std::vector, std::unique_ptr) and write none of the five.

Rule of Zero in practice

Rule of Five, spelled out

What declaring one member suppresses

You declare…Default ctorCopy opsMove ops
NothingGeneratedGeneratedGenerated
Any constructorNot generatedGeneratedGenerated
DestructorGeneratedGenerated (deprecated)Not generated → moves become copies
Copy ctor or copy assignment—The other is generated (deprecated)Not generated
Move ctor or move assignment—DeletedThe other is not generated
Watch out

Adding an empty ~T() {} “for logging” silently removes a class's move operations: every “move” becomes a copy. If you must declare a destructor, also = default the move and copy operations.

Explain the Rule of Zero.

Classes that aren't specifically resource managers shouldn't declare any of the special member functions. Let RAII members (containers, smart pointers, strings) handle ownership; the compiler-generated copy/move/destructor then do the right thing, and the code is shorter and exception-safe.
